Chapter 5: Living in a World That Refuses to Understand
You know, every single day, we’re reminded—sometimes in subtle ways, sometimes not so subtle—that some bodies just aren’t welcome. It’s in the way public spaces are designed, and in the little looks or offhand comments from strangers. The world keeps sending the same message: you’re too much, you don’t fit, you’re a problem to be solved.
And if you live in a larger body, you know this isn’t just an idea—it’s something you feel, every day.
Think about travel for a second. For some, hopping on a plane is just routine. For others, it’s a minefield of little indignities. Airplane seats? They’re built for smaller frames, so even getting seated can feel like a public performance. The anxiety doesn’t start at the gate—it creeps in long before you even pack your bag. Will the seatbelt fit this time? Will someone complain about sharing space? Will you end up being the center of an uncomfortable scene? Every journey becomes a test of endurance—a reminder that for some, comfort is a luxury, not a given.
Shopping for clothes isn’t any easier. Most stores? They just don’t carry sizes that work, and if they do, those pieces are tucked away in some out-of-sight corner. The choices are few, and the styles? Honestly, they’re rarely flattering. It’s like the world is whispering, “You’re not supposed to be here.”
Even something as simple as buying a dress turns into this emotional rollercoaster—frustration, shame, and sometimes just plain exhaustion.
Let’s talk about relationships. Navigating romance gets complicated by all these realities. There’s always that fear— Will I be rejected? Will someone see me as less desirable? Society’s narrow ideas of beauty can make it tough to really believe in your own worth.
But here’s the thing—desire doesn’t just vanish. That longing for connection and intimacy is still there. It takes so much courage and patience to put yourself out there, knowing you might get hurt.
And work? That’s not a safe haven either. Fatness is so often tied to negative assumptions—laziness, lack of willpower. Opportunities can be limited, promotions just out of reach. The pressure to shrink yourself, to blend in, never really lets up. So many end up working twice as hard, just trying to prove they belong.
But here’s something powerful—despite all of it, a quiet resilience starts to grow. Every act of survival, every moment you refuse to disappear, becomes a tiny act of rebellion. And over time, it gets a little easier to imagine a world where every body is welcome. Where being different isn’t a problem—it’s just part of being human.
The journey’s far from over, and the challenges are real. But hope? It sticks around.
